meta.titre: Monopolistic Competition: product differentiation, price and output
meta.sous_theme: Features, short-run and long-run equilibrium and comparison with monopoly

sections.contenu_markdown: Walk through any large market in Cameroon and you will find many tailors, restaurants or hairdressers selling similar services that each claim to be a little different from their neighbours. Each shop has some power to set its price, because customers have their favourite, yet a high price drives customers to the next stall. This mix of competition and market power is the subject of monopolistic competition. The paper asks for the features, the short-run and long-run equilibrium of the firm, and the difference from monopoly, usually in a question worth many marks.

items: Marginal revenue (MR) is the extra revenue from selling one more unit, and marginal cost (MC) is the extra cost of producing it.
A firm maximises profit at the output where MR equals MC.
Normal profit is the minimum reward needed to keep a firm in business; abnormal profit is any profit above it.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Features
| Feature | Monopolistic competition |
|---|---|
| Number of firms | Many, each with a small share of the market |
| Product | Differentiated by brand, quality, design, location or service, but close substitutes exist |
| Entry and exit | Relatively easy, no major barriers |
| Demand curve | Downward sloping and fairly elastic |
| Competition | Price and non-price (advertising, packaging, after-sales service) |
| Information | Imperfect: buyers do not know every price and quality |

Product differentiation is the defining feature: it gives each firm a small degree of market power. Examples are restaurants, hairdressing salons and tailoring workshops in a town.

### Short-run equilibrium
The firm maximises profit where **MR = MC**. Because the demand curve slopes downward, MR is below AR, and the price is read from the demand curve (AR) above the profit-maximising output. If AR exceeds AC, the firm earns abnormal profit; if AR is below AC, it makes a loss.

### Long-run equilibrium
Abnormal profit attracts new firms. They take customers away, so each firm's demand curve shifts to the left and becomes more elastic. Entry continues until AR just touches AC (tangency): each firm earns only **normal profit**, and MR = MC still holds at the equilibrium output. If firms make losses, some leave and demand for the remaining firms shifts right.

### Efficiency
Price exceeds marginal cost, so there is allocative inefficiency. The tangency occurs on the falling part of the AC curve, so output is below the level of lowest average cost: **excess capacity**. On the other hand consumers enjoy variety, and competition to improve products encourages innovation, although advertising raises costs.

### Comparison with monopoly
| | Monopoly | Monopolistic competition |
|---|---|---|
| Firms | One | Many |
| Barriers to entry | High | Low |
| Close substitutes | None | Many |
| Long-run profit | Abnormal profit can last | Normal profit only |
| Demand | Less elastic | More elastic |

variantes.nom: Question on short-run and long-run equilibrium
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks 'show how a firm determines price and output'.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Draw two labelled diagrams, one for each period. In the short run mark MR = MC to fix output, read the price from the demand curve and show the profit rectangle. In the long run show demand shifting to the left until it is tangent to AC. In a written answer give the same steps in words and, if possible, a numerical example.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question says 'differentiate between' or 'compare'.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Begin with a short definition of each market, then use pairs of contrasts (number of firms, barriers, substitutes, long-run profit, elasticity) and mention the similarities: both face a downward-sloping demand curve, both set MR = MC and both charge a price above marginal cost.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A tailoring workshop in a town faces the demand curve $P=100-2Q$, where $P$ is the price in thousand FCFA per outfit and $Q$ is the number of outfits per month. Its total cost is $TC=200+20Q$ (thousand FCFA).

(a) Find the profit-maximising output, price and profit.
(b) New tailors enter the market and the demand curve of the workshop becomes $P=60-2Q$. Find the new equilibrium and the profit.
(c) Comment on the efficiency of the long-run position.

etapes.action: Derive marginal revenue and marginal cost.
etapes.justification: Total revenue is $PQ=100Q-2Q^2$, so marginal revenue is its slope; MC is the slope of total cost.

etapes.action: Equate MR and MC and read the price from demand.
etapes.justification: Profit is maximised where MR = MC.

etapes.resultat_markdown: $AC=\frac{200+400}{20}=30$, so profit $=(60-30)\times20=600$ thousand FCFA per month.

etapes.justification: Entry shifts demand to the left; the profit-maximising rule is unchanged.
At tangency, price equals average cost.
Compare price with MC and average cost with the cost at a larger output.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $P=40>MC=20$, so allocative inefficiency. At 20 outfits, $AC=30$ is lower than $40$, so the firm has excess capacity.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Answers**: (a) $Q=20$, $P=$ 60 thousand FCFA, profit **600 thousand FCFA** per month; (b) $Q=10$, $P=$ 40 thousand FCFA, profit **0** (normal profit); (c) in the long run the price is above marginal cost and output is below the level that minimises average cost, so the workshop is inefficient, though customers keep a wide variety of outfits.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing products in monopolistic competition as identical.
items.pourquoi_faux: Identical products belong to perfect competition; here differentiation gives some market power.
items.correction_markdown: Write that products are differentiated but close substitutes.

items.erreur_markdown: Setting output where price equals marginal cost.
items.pourquoi_faux: That is the rule in perfect competition. The firm has a downward-sloping demand curve.
items.correction_markdown: Find output where MR = MC, then read the price from the demand curve.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that abnormal profit continues in the long run because the firm has some monopoly power.
items.pourquoi_faux: Entry is easy, so new firms reduce demand until only normal profit remains.
items.correction_markdown: State that entry eliminates abnormal profit and demand shifts to tangency with AC.

items.erreur_markdown: Drawing the MR curve above the demand curve.
items.pourquoi_faux: With a downward-sloping demand curve, MR lies below AR.
items.correction_markdown: Draw MR below AR, steeper, and label every curve.

items.enonce_markdown: State four features of monopolistic competition and give two ways in which a firm can differentiate its product.
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each feature: many firms; differentiated products; easy entry and exit; downward-sloping, fairly elastic demand; non-price competition; imperfect information. Award marks for two ways: branding or packaging, quality or design, location, opening hours, customer service or advertising.

items.enonce_markdown: A firm in monopolistic competition faces $P=90-3Q$ (thousand FCFA per unit, $Q$ in units per month) and has total cost $TC=75+30Q$ (thousand FCFA). (a) Find output, price and profit in the short run. (b) Explain what will happen in the long run.
items.solution_markdown: (a) $MR=90-6Q$ and $MC=30$, so $Q=$ **10**. The price is $90-30=$ **60**. $AC=\frac{75+300}{10}=37.5$, so profit $=(60-37.5)\times10=$ **225 thousand FCFA**. (b) The abnormal profit attracts new firms; the demand curve of this firm shifts left and becomes more elastic until price equals average cost, leaving normal profit only.

items.enonce_markdown: A firm in monopolistic competition has total cost $TC=75+30Q$ (thousand FCFA). In the long run it faces the demand curve $P=60-3Q$ (thousand FCFA per unit, $Q$ in units per month). (a) Show that the firm earns normal profit. (b) Calculate the gap between price and marginal cost. (c) To what extent is monopolistic competition efficient?
items.solution_markdown: (a) $MR=60-6Q=30$ gives $Q=5$ and $P=60-15=45$; $AC=30+\frac{75}{5}=45$, so price equals average cost and profit is **zero** (normal profit). (b) The gap is $45-30=$ **15 thousand FCFA** per unit, which shows allocative inefficiency. (c) A balanced answer: it is not productively efficient (excess capacity) or allocatively efficient (price above MC), and advertising adds cost; but consumers get variety, firms can only earn normal profit in the long run, and rivalry encourages innovation and service. Conclude that it is less efficient than perfect competition in theory but may give more choice to consumers.

items_markdown: Monopolistic competition has many firms, differentiated products, easy entry and exit, and a downward-sloping demand curve.
Short run: output where MR = MC, price from the demand curve; abnormal profit or loss is possible.
Long run: entry or exit moves demand until AR is tangent to AC and the firm earns normal profit.
Price is above marginal cost and output is below the lowest-cost level (excess capacity), but consumers gain variety.
Compared with monopoly it has many firms, low barriers, many close substitutes, more elastic demand and no lasting abnormal profit.
